Particular Providence
pur-TIK-yuh-ler PROV-i-duhns
doctrinal phrase
From particular (concerning individual things) and providence (God’s governing care); the doctrine that God governs every detail of His creation.

Biblical Definition

Particular providence is the doctrine that God’s providential government extends not only to the great course of the world in general but to every particular creature, event, and circumstance, down to the smallest detail. Against the deist, who allows a general providence by which God upholds the laws of nature but denies His care for individual things, and against the Epicurean, who attributes all to chance, Scripture teaches that God numbers the very hairs of the head, that not a sparrow falls to the ground without the Father, that the lot is cast into the lap but its whole disposing is of the LORD, and that He works all things after the counsel of His own will. Nothing is too great for His power nor too small for His care; the rise and fall of empires and the falling of a sparrow are alike under His hand. This providence is wise, holy, and good, governing even the sins of men and the malice of devils to serve His purposes, without Himself being the author of sin, and it works all things together for good to them that love God. The dictionary holds particular providence as a chief comfort of the believer and a rebuke to the practical deism of the age. The Christian does not live in a world of chance or of an absentee God, but under the constant, detailed, fatherly government of his God, who orders every circumstance of his life—his griefs and his joys, his losses and his gains—for his good and God’s glory. To believe in particular providence is to rest in the truth that nothing befalls the child of God by accident, but all by the wise and loving appointment of his Father.

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that God governs every particular creature and event, down to the smallest detail—the falling sparrow, the numbered hairs—against deism and chance; a chief comfort of the believer.

Modern Corruption

Deism allows only a general providence and denies God’s care for particulars, leaving the believer to chance and an absentee God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is deism, ancient and modern, which allows that God made the world and upholds its general laws but denies that He governs particular events and cares for individual things—leaving the details of life to chance, nature, or the creature’s own management. Scripture refutes it: God numbers the hairs of the head, not a sparrow falls without the Father, the lot’s whole disposing is of the LORD, and He works all things after the counsel of His will. Nothing is too small for His care nor too great for His power.

The practical deism of the age is the more dangerous because it often coexists with an orthodox confession. Many who would never deny providence in word live as though their lives were ruled by chance, luck, or their own contriving, and meet trouble as though their Father had forgotten them. The dictionary holds particular providence as a chief comfort and a summons to faith. The believer lives under the constant, detailed, fatherly government of God, who orders every circumstance—grief and joy, loss and gain—for his good and God’s glory. To rest in particular providence is to know that nothing befalls the child of God by accident, but all by the wise and loving appointment of his Father, who works even the worst to good.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase names God’s government of every particular thing, against deism and chance, the believer’s comfort in every circumstance.

expand to see more

“Particular” — concerning individual creatures and events, not merely the general course.

Latin providentia — foresight, provision, governing care.

The falling sparrow and the numbered hairs picture its reach.

Governs even sin and evil to God’s ends, without authoring sin.

Set against deism (general-only) and Epicurean chance.

Usage

"Particular providence is preached against deism and the practical deism of the age."

"The falling sparrow and numbered hairs are its classic proofs."

"It is held as the believer’s comfort that nothing befalls him by accident."
